verdict.rationale: The torment vocabulary in Revelation is lexically strong for an unending conscious state. The verb 'to torment' (basanizo) is joined with the phrase 'unto the ages of the ages' (eis tous aionas ton aionon) in Revelation 20:10. The noun 'torment' (basanismos) is paired with the negated phrase 'they have no rest day and night' (anapausin ouk echousin hemeras kai nuktos) in Revelation 14:11. Matthew 25:46 binds 'eternal punishment' (kolasin aionion) to 'eternal life' (zoen aionion) under one adjective 'eternal' (aionios) so the duration claim is symmetrical. The pattern is materially contested because the canon also names the final state with destruction vocabulary: 'destruction' (olethros) in 2 Thessalonians 1:9, 'to destroy' (apollymi) of soul and body in Gehenna (the place of final judgment) in Matthew 10:28, 'destruction' (apoleia) in Philippians 3:19 and 2 Peter 3:7, and second-death 'death' (thanatos) in Revelation 20:14. Also 'eternal' (aionios) in this canon also qualifies completed-event nouns like 'eternal judgment' (krima aionion) in Hebrews 6:2 and 'eternal redemption' (lytrosis aioniou) in Hebrews 9:12, so it can denote permanence of result rather than ongoing process. Two defensible lexical readings coexist; the words and grammar do not rank them.

scripture.reasoning: The phrase 'eternal punishment' (kolasin aionion) stands in deliberate grammatical parallel with 'eternal life' (zoen aionion) in one balanced sentence, the single adjective 'eternal' (aionios) governing both nouns. Whatever duration sense the adjective bears in the second clause it must bear in the first, because one word in one clause cannot carry two divergent temporal senses. The lexical caveat is that 'punishment' (kolasis) is a low-frequency noun in the canon, only 2 occurrences, the other in 1 John 4:18 of present fear, so its substantive sense cannot be triangulated against many parallel uses.

The phrase 'the smoke of their torment goes up unto ages of ages' (ho kapnos tou basanismou auton eis aionas aionon anabainei) is joined with 'and they have no rest day and night' (kai ouk echousin anapausin hemeras kai nuktos). The rising smoke plus the explicit denial of rest by day and by night reads as an ongoing conscious experience. The lexical caveat is that the noun 'torment' (basanismos) in the canon occurs only 6 times and all 6 are in Revelation, in the apocalyptic genre (highly symbolic visionary literature about end-time events) where heavy symbolism is the norm.

The phrase 'and they will be tormented day and night unto the ages of the ages' (kai basanisthesontai hemeras kai nuktos eis tous aionas ton aionon). The future passive of the verb 'to torment' (basanizo) with the strongest duration phrase the canon possesses describes the devil, the beast, and the false prophet under torment without terminus. The subjects here are non-human cosmic agents, which is the lexical caveat conditionalists (those who hold that immortality is granted only to the saved) press when generalizing the verse to human unbelievers.

The phrase 'where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched' (hopou ho skolex auton ou teleuta kai to pyr ou sbennytai) quotes Isaiah 66:24. The two negated verbs and 'unquenchable' (asbeston) in verse 43 mark the agents of judgment as perpetual. The noun 'worm' (skolex) is a hapax legomenon (a word that occurs only once) in the New Testament, only this single occurrence, so its sense is anchored only to its Isaiah donor text, where in the source context the worm and fire act on 'corpses' (ptomata). Whether the perpetuity attaches to the sufferer's consciousness or only to the consuming agents is precisely the disputed point.

The phrase 'eternal destruction away from the presence of the Lord' (olethron aionion apo prosopou tou kyriou). The head noun is 'destruction' or 'ruin' (olethros), only 4 occurrences in the canon and never elsewhere a torment word. The adjective 'eternal' (aionion) can be read as eternal in result, on analogy with the same adjective in Hebrews 6:2 'eternal judgment' (krima aionion) and Hebrews 9:12 'eternal redemption' (lytrosin aionian), both event-nouns where the adjective denotes permanence of the act's result. This is the strongest single lexical foothold for a conditionalist reading and the principal reason the verdict is disputed.

The phrase 'undergoing the penalty of eternal fire' (pyros aioniou diken hypechousai), with Sodom and Gomorrah set forth as an 'example' (deigma). The cities are no longer burning, so 'eternal' (aionion) fire here describes the enduring result of destruction rather than an observable ongoing burning. Annihilationists (those who hold that the unsaved are finally destroyed rather than kept conscious forever) press this as a near-context lexical analogy for the final judgment fire vocabulary.

The phrase 'fear the One able to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna' (phobeisthe de mallon ton dynamenon kai psychen kai soma apolesai en geenne). The verb is 'to destroy' (apollymi), the destruction word group, with both 'soul' (psyche) and 'body' (soma) as direct objects, and 'Gehenna' (geenna, the place of final judgment) as the location. The lexical caveat for the eternal conscious torment (ECT) reading is that 'to destroy' (apollymi) can mean 'perish' or 'be lost' as well as 'terminate', and the construction does not by itself force either reading. For conditionalism it is the strongest synoptic foothold pairing destruction vocabulary with the soul and Gehenna.

The phrase 'this is the second death, the lake of fire' (houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin, he limne tou pyros). The narrator gives the lake of fire a name and the name is 'death' (thanatos). Conditionalists read this as a definitional gloss in which the canon supplies its own equation of the final state with death, the cessation language. Readers who hold eternal conscious torment (ECT) take 'second death' as a state, a separation analogous to spiritual death rather than extinction. Lexically the equation is given but not expounded.

The phrase 'eternal judgment' (krimatos aioniou). The head noun is 'judgment' (krima), an act of judgment, not a process, and the same adjective 'eternal' (aionios) describes its result-permanence rather than an unending courtroom procedure. This is a parallel lexical use within Hebrews that demonstrates 'eternal' (aionios) in the canon can qualify a completed-event noun and denote permanence of outcome, which is the linguistic move conditionalists apply to 'eternal destruction' (olethros aionion) in 2 Thessalonians 1:9.

complicating_texts.resolution: The phrase 'eternal destruction' (olethron aionion) uses 'destruction' or 'ruin' (olethros) as its head noun. The adjective 'eternal' (aionios) is the same word used in Hebrews 6:2 ('eternal judgment', krima aionion) and Hebrews 9:12 ('eternal redemption', lytrosin aionian) to describe completed acts whose RESULT is permanent. Conditionalists read this canonical pattern back into 2 Thessalonians 1:9 as annihilation of eternal result, separation as cessation rather than as continued conscious existence. The eternal conscious torment reading takes 'eternal' (aionion) adverbially of unending duration and reads 'destruction' (olethros) as ruinous, persistent separation from the Lord's presence. Both are grammatically defensible from the lexical data alone, so the text complicates a clean affirmation.

The phrase 'eternal fire' (pyros aioniou) with Sodom presented as 'example' (deigma) is read by annihilationists as evidence that 'eternal' (aionios) fire denotes a permanent outcome of destruction, since Sodom is not presently burning. The eternal conscious torment reading distinguishes the fire's visible effect on cities from the fate of persons and points to Revelation 14:11 and Revelation 20:10 for the personal-consciousness datum. The lexical analogy cannot by itself settle which referent governs, leaving the matter contested.

The phrase 'the worm does not die' (skolex ou teleuta) and 'the fire is not quenched' (pyr ou sbennytai) quote Isaiah 66:24, where in the donor text the worm and fire act on 'corpses' (ptomata), which conditionalists take to support consumption rather than living torment. The noun 'worm' (skolex) is a New Testament hapax legomenon (a word that occurs only once in the New Testament), so its sense is fixed by Isaiah alone. The eternal conscious torment reading takes the perpetual worm and unquenchable fire as agents that never cease acting on a still-suffering object. The lexicon supports the perpetuity of the agents but does not by itself specify perpetual consciousness of the object.

The form 'to destroy' (apolesai, aorist infinitive (a completed-action verb form) of apollymi) with both 'soul' (psyche) and 'body' (soma) as objects, located 'in Gehenna' (en geenne, the place of final judgment), places the destruction word group on the same object that the eternal conscious torment reading expects to be eternally conscious. Conditionalists read 'to destroy' (apollymi) here in its strong sense, terminate, and treat the pairing of soul and body as comprehensive cessation. The eternal conscious torment reading appeals to the range of 'to destroy' (apollymi), which elsewhere can mean lost or ruined rather than annihilated (Matthew 18:11 of lost persons; Luke 15 of lost coin, sheep, son who is restored). The verb's polysemy (the property of a word carrying multiple senses) is the lexical reason this verse alone does not settle the question.

The phrase 'this is the second death' (houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin) equates the lake of fire with 'death' (thanatos), in the canon's own gloss. Conditionalists treat the canon-supplied equation as authoritative: the final state IS death, the cessation language. The eternal conscious torment reading takes 'second death' as a category of separation from God analogous to spiritual death in Ephesians 2:1, a state of permanent ruin rather than extinction. The narrative equation is plain; what is contested is whether 'death' (thanatos) here keeps its ordinary cessation sense or carries a metaphorical separation sense.

variant_units_examined.note: Verses 44 and 46, which repeat the worm-and-fire refrain, are absent from the earliest witnesses (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) and are widely regarded as harmonizations from verse 48. Their omission does not change the verdict because verse 48 retains the refrain in all major critical editions.
The pair 'eternal punishment' (kolasin aionion) and 'eternal life' (zoen aionion) is textually stable across the principal critical editions; no material variant unit affects the duration parallel.

variants.note: No ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) was consulted; New Testament outside 3 John is treated as ecm-shadow. The cited torment, destruction, and second-death phrases are textually stable in the principal critical editions.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The verb 'to torment' (basanizo) plus the phrase 'unto ages of ages' (eis aionas aionon) and the negated 'they have no rest' (anapausin ouk echousin) in Revelation 14:11 and Revelation 20:10, joined with the 'eternal punishment' (kolasin aionion) and 'eternal life' (zoen aionion) parallel in Matthew 25:46 governed by one adjective 'eternal' (aionios), are read as unending conscious suffering. The duration vocabulary in Revelation is the strongest in the canon, and the symmetry in Matthew forecloses an asymmetric duration claim.

The phrase 'eternal destruction' (olethros aionios) in 2 Thessalonians 1:9, the verb 'to destroy' (apollymi) of soul and body in Gehenna (the place of final judgment) in Matthew 10:28, the noun 'destruction' (apoleia) in 2 Peter 3:7 and Philippians 3:19, and the second-death equation in Revelation 20:14 read as the destruction or cessation of the unsaved, with 'eternal' (aionios) denoting permanence of result on the model of 'eternal judgment' (krima aionion) in Hebrews 6:2 and 'eternal redemption' (lytrosin aionian) in Hebrews 9:12. Immortality is granted only to the redeemed.

The phrase 'eternal' (aionios) fire in Jude 1:7 (Sodom no longer burning) is taken as a permanent-result idiom for fire vocabulary, and Revelation's torment imagery is read as apocalyptic symbol (visionary symbolic language) of definitive overthrow rather than a literal duration statement about persons. The destruction word group across the epistles is read as ranking the cessation pattern.

The adjective 'eternal' (aionios) is treated as derived from the noun 'age' (aion), with an age-defined rather than absolute-eternity sense in some contexts. For example Matthew 12:32 'neither in this age nor in the coming one' (hina mete en touto to aioni mete en to mellonti). The noun 'punishment' (kolasis), with its lexical range including corrective discipline, is read as remedial rather than terminal. The lexical foothold for this lens is narrower than the other two and turns on contested glosses of 'age' (aion) and 'punishment' (kolasis).

hermeneutics.notes: The disagreement is not over whether judgment is real or final but over whether the lexical duration markers attach to ongoing consciousness or to permanence of outcome. The Revelation torment vocabulary and the synoptic and epistolary destruction vocabulary pull in different directions within the same canon, and 'eternal' (aionios) has attested uses in this canon for both unending process ('eternal life', zoe aionios) and permanent result ('eternal judgment' krima aionion, 'eternal redemption' lytrosis aionian).

stem_audit.neutralized_form: What is the lexical duration and nature of the final state of the unsaved as described by the relevant Greek terms: 'eternal' (aionios), 'to torment' / 'torment' (basanizo / basanismos), 'punishment' (kolasis), 'destruction' (olethros), 'to destroy' / 'destruction' (apollymi / apoleia), 'death' / second death (thanatos)?
stem_audit.notes: VERDICT-CHANGED: The original stem clause 'as the just judgment of a holy God' embeds an evaluative theological frame, and 'eternal, conscious punishment' presupposes the contested outcome (unending consciousness rather than cessation or restoration). The verdict is derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form isolates the testable lexical question so the destruction-vocabulary and result-permanence readings receive fair weight.

lay_summary: The Greek vocabulary across these passages pulls in two directions at once, which is why the lexical picture is disputed rather than settled. On one side, the torment vocabulary is strong. In Revelation 14:11 the smoke of their torment (basanismos) goes up to ages of ages, and they have no rest day or night, and Revelation 20:10 says they will be tormented day and night unto the ages of the ages, using the verb 'to torment' (basanizo) with the strongest duration phrase the language has. Matthew 25:46 places eternal punishment and eternal life side by side with the very same adjective 'eternal' (aionios), so the punishment seems to last as long as the life. Mark 9:48 adds that the worm (skolex) does not die and the fire is not quenched. On the other side, the destruction vocabulary complicates this. 2 Thessalonians 1:9 speaks of eternal destruction using the noun 'destruction' or 'ruin' (olethros), not a torment word. Matthew 10:28 warns of the One able to destroy (apollymi) both soul and body in Gehenna (the place of final judgment), putting the destruction verb on the soul itself. Revelation 20:14 names the lake of fire as the second death (thanatos). Jude 7 calls Sodom an example of eternal fire, yet Sodom is no longer burning, which suggests that 'eternal' (aionios) can describe a permanent result rather than an unending process. Hebrews 6:2 confirms this elsewhere, calling judgment itself eternal (aionion), an event with permanent result, not an unending courtroom. Readers who hold to unending conscious suffering lean on the torment texts. Readers who hold to conditional immortality or annihilation lean on the destruction texts and the canon's own usage of aionios for permanent result. Both readings can be defended from the words themselves, so the lexical evidence supports a real and final judgment but does not by itself decide between unending consciousness and final destruction. The stem also assumes the consciousness conclusion, so the testable lexical question was isolated separately.
